mode_evidence: Iamblichus says the divine light shines on the luminous vehicle of the soul and moves the faculty of imagination (phantasia), while attention and reason stay conscious. The light is thus received in the imaginal faculty yet also named as light brought through sun, moon, air, water or a wall. Book II separately grades luminosity and fire seen at epiphanies as visible appearances.
onset_evidence: No technique for breaking through is given. Methods listed (darkness, sun or moon light, open air, water, a prepared wall, chants) are only vehicles; the light comes from the will of the gods, who shine through whatever instruments they choose. The Chaldean Oracles quoted by Wilder say one should not invoke the vision before the body is perfected or initiated.

conditions.setting: darkness, open air, sun or moon light, water, or a wall prepared with sacred engraved figures
conditions.prerequisites: the gods' will; priestly preparation; initiation per the Oracles
conditions.other: the light is fixed in a solid place so it is not widely diffused

stages.label: grades of light at epiphanies
stages.description: Images of gods are replete with fulgid light, archangels supernaturally luminous, angels luminous, demons a turbid or smouldering fire, souls partial gleams; the fire of the gods is stable, that of angels in motion, that of demons unstable.

what_to_do_with_light: Receive it; the seer stays attentive and awake. It is not to be produced by technique.
cautions: Chaldean Oracles: do not invoke the Autoptic Image of Being before the body is perfected or initiated
The light is from the gods, not the operator's art
interpretation: A single faculty, the 'bringing of light' (photagogia): divine light illuminating the soul's aether-like vehicle and moving the imagination, whatever the outward medium.
practice_summary: Iamblichus describes rather than prescribes. Diviners who stay conscious are lit from the gods by one faculty, the bringing of light. The outward means are darkness as an auxiliary, the light of sun or moon, the open air, chants prepared for the god's coming, conducting light through water, or letting it shine on a wall prepared with sacred engraved figures and fixed in a solid place so it does not diffuse. Attention and reason remain aware while the fancy is moved by the gods. The light is external, undivided and subject only to the gods' will, so none of these means compels it. A Damascius note describes a woman who poured pure water into a glass cup and saw luminous appearances of future events in it.
